questions.subject: MICROECONOMICS
questions.learningObjective: identify the effect of a binding price ceiling
questions.stem: A binding price ceiling is set below the equilibrium price. What is the most likely result?

options.misconception: confuses a price ceiling with a price floor
confuses who gains and who loses from a ceiling

questions.explanation: A price ceiling below equilibrium makes the price artificially low, so quantity demanded exceeds quantity supplied, creating a shortage. A price floor would create a surplus, a non-binding ceiling would have no effect, and producer surplus falls rather than rises.

questions.subject: MICROECONOMICS
questions.learningObjective: identify the effect of a binding price floor
questions.stem: A binding price floor is set above the equilibrium price. What is the most likely result?

options.misconception: confuses a price floor with a price ceiling
confuses who gains and who loses from a floor

questions.explanation: A price floor above equilibrium raises price above the market-clearing level, so quantity supplied exceeds quantity demanded and a surplus results. A ceiling would create a shortage, a non-binding floor has no effect, and consumer surplus falls rather than rises.

questions.subject: MICROECONOMICS
questions.learningObjective: predict price and quantity after a demand increase
questions.stem: If consumer demand increases while supply is unchanged, what happens to equilibrium price and quantity?

options.misconception: confuses a demand increase with a supply increase
reverses the quantity effect of demand

questions.explanation: An increase in demand shifts the demand curve right. With supply unchanged, the new intersection occurs at a higher price and a larger quantity. Options B, C, and D describe effects of other shifts or incorrect directions.

questions.subject: MICROECONOMICS
questions.learningObjective: predict price and quantity after a supply increase
questions.stem: If supply increases while demand is unchanged, what happens to equilibrium price and quantity?

options.misconception: confuses a supply increase with a demand increase
confuses a supply increase with a demand decrease

questions.explanation: An increase in supply shifts the supply curve right. With demand unchanged, equilibrium price falls and equilibrium quantity rises. The other options reverse or misattribute the shift.

questions.subject: MICROECONOMICS
questions.learningObjective: distinguish binding from non-binding price ceilings
questions.stem: A price ceiling is set above the equilibrium price. What is its effect on the market?

options.text: It is non-binding and has no effect

options.misconception: confuses a ceiling with a floor
assumes the ceiling changes the market price

questions.explanation: A ceiling above equilibrium is not binding because the market price is already below it, so the market clears normally. A binding ceiling below equilibrium would create a shortage; a floor would create a surplus.
questions.hint: Compare the ceiling to equilibrium price.

questions.learningObjective: describe a shortage and its price pressure
questions.stem: When quantity demanded exceeds quantity supplied at the current price, the market has a
questions.explanation: Excess demand is a shortage. Unsatisfied buyers bid price up, moving the market toward equilibrium. A surplus is excess supply, equilibrium has no pressure, and a binding ceiling is one possible cause rather than the outcome.

questions.learningObjective: describe a surplus and its price pressure
questions.stem: When quantity supplied exceeds quantity demanded at the current price, the market has a
questions.explanation: Excess supply is a surplus. Sellers cut prices, moving the market toward equilibrium. A shortage is excess demand, equilibrium has no pressure, and a binding floor is one possible cause rather than the outcome.

questions.subject: MICROECONOMICS
questions.learningObjective: distinguish movement along a curve from a shift
questions.stem: A change in the good's own price causes

options.text: A shift of the supply curve
A shift of the demand curve
options.misconception: confuses own-price change with non-price determinant

options.text: A movement along the demand curve

questions.explanation: Own-price changes move along an existing demand curve. Non-price factors such as income or tastes shift the curve. Supply shifts come from cost or technology changes, not from the good's own price.

questions.subject: MICROECONOMICS
questions.learningObjective: identify a demand shift for a normal good
questions.stem: For a normal good, an increase in consumer income most likely

options.misconception: attributes a demand determinant to supply
treats a normal good as inferior

questions.explanation: For a normal good, higher income increases demand at every price, shifting demand right. An inferior good would shift left; own-price changes move along the curve; income does not shift supply.
questions.hint: Is the good normal or inferior?

questions.subject: MICROECONOMICS
questions.learningObjective: identify a supply shift from higher input costs
questions.stem: If production input costs rise, the supply curve most likely

options.misconception: confuses higher costs with lower costs
confuses input cost with own price
attributes a supply determinant to demand

questions.explanation: Higher input costs reduce profitability at each price, shifting supply left. Lower costs would shift right; own-price changes move along the curve; input costs do not directly shift demand.

questions.subject: MICROECONOMICS
questions.stem: Demand increases and supply decreases at the same time. Which outcome is certain?
questions.explanation: Higher demand pushes price up, and lower supply also pushes price up, so price certainly rises. Quantity is ambiguous because demand raises it while supply lowers it. Options B and C each assume one quantity effect dominates, and D ignores both price effects.

questions.subject: MICROECONOMICS
questions.stem: Demand and supply both increase at the same time. Which outcome is certain?
questions.explanation: Both an increase in demand and an increase in supply push quantity up, so quantity certainly rises. Price is ambiguous because demand raises it while supply lowers it. Options B and C each assume one price effect dominates, and D ignores both quantity effects.

questions.subject: MICROECONOMICS
questions.stem: Market equilibrium occurs when

options.text: Price is at its legal maximum

questions.explanation: Equilibrium is the price and quantity at which quantity demanded equals quantity supplied. A price ceiling is a policy, not a market outcome; surplus can exist in equilibrium; and excess supply describes a surplus.

questions.stem: The law of demand states that, ceteris paribus,

options.text: Price and quantity demanded are inversely related
Price and quantity demanded are directly related
options.misconception: states the law of supply instead

options.text: Income and quantity demanded are inversely related
Price and quantity supplied are inversely related

questions.explanation: The law of demand says quantity demanded falls when price rises, holding other factors constant. Option B is the law of supply; income effects depend on normal or inferior goods; and inverse price-quantity supplied is not a standard law.

questions.stem: The law of supply states that, ceteris paribus,

options.text: Price and quantity supplied are directly related
Price and quantity supplied are inversely related
Price and quantity demanded are directly related
Income and quantity supplied are directly related

questions.explanation: The law of supply says quantity supplied rises when price rises, holding other factors constant. Option B reverses it, C describes demand incorrectly, and income is not the own-price determinant in the law of supply.

questions.subject: MICROECONOMICS
questions.stem: Price rises by 5 percent and quantity demanded falls by 10 percent. What is the price elasticity of demand?
questions.explanation: Price elasticity of demand is the absolute value of percent change in quantity demanded divided by percent change in price: |-10% / 5%| = 2.
questions.hint: Use absolute value of the ratio.

questions.stem: Demand is inelastic when the absolute value of price elasticity of demand is
questions.explanation: Inelastic demand means quantity responds less than proportionally to price, so |Ed| < 1. Elastic demand has |Ed| > 1, unit elastic has 1, and perfectly elastic has infinity.

questions.subject: MICROECONOMICS
questions.stem: Demand is unit elastic when the absolute value of price elasticity of demand is
questions.explanation: Unit elastic demand means quantity changes by the same percentage as price, so |Ed| = 1. Elastic demand has |Ed| > 1, inelastic demand has |Ed| < 1, and perfectly inelastic demand has 0.

questions.subject: MICROECONOMICS
questions.stem: A vertical demand curve represents

options.misconception: confuses a vertical curve with unit elasticity

questions.explanation: A vertical demand curve means quantity demanded does not change when price changes, so demand is perfectly inelastic. A horizontal curve is perfectly elastic, and unit elasticity is not represented by a vertical line.

questions.subject: MICROECONOMICS
questions.stem: A horizontal demand curve represents

options.misconception: confuses a horizontal curve with unit elasticity

questions.explanation: A horizontal demand curve means consumers will buy any quantity at one price but none at a higher price, so demand is perfectly elastic. A vertical curve is perfectly inelastic, and unit elasticity is not represented by a horizontal line.

questions.learningObjective: apply total revenue rule for elastic demand
questions.stem: If demand is elastic, a decrease in price will
questions.explanation: With elastic demand, the percentage increase in quantity demanded exceeds the percentage decrease in price, so total revenue rises. Inelastic demand would lower revenue, unit elastic demand would leave it unchanged, and producer surplus is a separate concept.
questions.hint: Compare percentage quantity change to price change.

questions.learningObjective: apply total revenue rule for inelastic demand
questions.stem: If demand is inelastic, a decrease in price will
questions.explanation: With inelastic demand, the percentage increase in quantity demanded is smaller than the percentage decrease in price, so total revenue falls. Elastic demand would raise revenue, unit elastic demand would leave it unchanged, and consumer surplus is a separate concept.
questions.hint: Compare percentage quantity change to price change.

questions.stem: A positive cross-price elasticity of demand indicates that the two goods are

options.misconception: zero cross-price elasticity indicates unrelated goods

questions.explanation: A positive cross-price elasticity means an increase in the price of one good raises demand for the other, the definition of substitutes. Complements have negative cross-price elasticity, unrelated goods have zero, and inferior goods are identified by income elasticity.

questions.stem: A negative income elasticity of demand indicates that the good is

luxury goods have income elasticity greater than 1

questions.explanation: Negative income elasticity means demand falls when income rises, the definition of an inferior good. Normal goods have positive income elasticity, substitutes are identified by cross-price elasticity, and luxury goods have income elasticity greater than 1.

questions.subject: MICROECONOMICS
questions.learningObjective: compute consumer surplus from a linear demand curve
questions.stem: Demand is P = 10 - Q and the market price is 4. What is consumer surplus?
questions.explanation: At price 4, quantity demanded is 6. Consumer surplus is the triangle with base 6 and height 10 - 4 = 6, so 0.5 * 6 * 6 = 18.
questions.hint: Find quantity at the price, then triangle area.

questions.subject: MICROECONOMICS
questions.stem: Consumer surplus is the difference between

options.text: Actual price paid and marginal cost
Willingness to pay and actual price paid

questions.explanation: Consumer surplus measures the net benefit to buyers: willingness to pay minus the price actually paid. Producer surplus compares price to marginal cost, profit compares revenue to cost, and price times quantity is not surplus.

questions.subject: MICROECONOMICS
questions.stem: Producer surplus is the difference between

options.text: Willingness to pay and price paid

questions.explanation: Producer surplus measures the net benefit to sellers: the price received minus marginal cost. Consumer surplus compares willingness to pay to price, and revenue minus fixed cost is not producer surplus.

questions.stem: The side of the market with the more inelastic curve bears a larger share of a tax. This principle is

options.misconception: confuses tax burden with buyer benefit
confuses tax burden with seller benefit

questions.explanation: Tax incidence describes how the burden of a tax is divided between buyers and sellers based on relative elasticities. Consumer surplus and producer surplus measure benefits, while deadweight loss measures the efficiency cost of a tax.
questions.hint: What term describes tax burden sharing?
